### Long-Term Care: How You Can Financially Prepare for the Expense
URL: /resources/long-term-care-how-you-can-financially-prepare-for-the-expen-2

A farm couple in their late 60s can have a paid-off operation, a healthy retirement account, and still be one hip fracture away from a financial crisis. Long-term care is the expense most families underestimate twice: they guess the price too low, and they guess how soon they'll need a plan too far off. By the time care starts, the options for paying for it have already narrowed. Treating long-term care as a funding decision you make in your 50s and 60s, not a scramble you handle in your 80s, is what separates families who stay in control of their assets from families who don't.

Here in Brookings, this conversation comes up constantly with farm families thinking about the next generation and with professional service owners planning their own retirement. It touches tax planning, entity structure, and often the same succession conversations we're already having about the operation itself.

## Why the price tag catches families off guard

A private room in a South Dakota nursing home commonly runs $80,000 to $100,000 a year, and assisted living facilities in the $50,000 to $65,000 range are typical across the Midwest. In-home care, which most people say they'd prefer, still costs $25 to $30 an hour once you're paying for skilled help beyond a few hours a week. None of that is a one-time bill. Care for a spouse with a progressive condition can run five to eight years.

The number that surprises people most is what Medicare will not cover. Medicare pays for short-term rehabilitation after a hospital stay, not for ongoing custodial care. Medicaid does cover long-term care, but only after a person has spent down most of their countable assets, which for a farm family can mean selling land or liquidating an operation they spent decades building. That's the scenario every strategy below is designed to avoid.

## Three ways to fund the cost, and what each one actually protects

Most families end up using some blend of three tools: long-term care insurance, VA benefits if a spouse or parent served, and self-funding from savings or farm assets. None of them is automatically the right answer. The right mix depends on age, health, military service, and how much of the family's net worth is tied up in land, equipment, or a business.

| Funding source | Best fit | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Long-term care insurance | Healthy applicants in their 50s to early 60s | Premiums can rise; underwriting gets harder after a diagnosis |
| VA Aid and Attendance benefit | Veterans and surviving spouses meeting service and income tests | Application can take months; asset and income limits apply |
| Self-funding | Families with liquid savings or a plan to protect farm/business assets | Requires real numbers, not a guess, years before care starts |

Long-term care insurance locks in a benefit while you're still insurable. Premiums are lower and underwriting is far easier for a healthy 55-year-old than a 70-year-old with a recent diagnosis. The tradeoff is cost certainty going the other direction: premiums aren't guaranteed to stay flat, and policies bought decades ago sometimes come due for a real increase right when a client is on a fixed income.

Self-funding works when the numbers are run honestly. That means knowing your actual liquid net worth, not your net worth on paper once land and equipment are included, and building a reserve that could cover four to six years of care without forcing a sale of the operation. This is where the analysis overlaps directly with entity structure and [multi entity farm tax strategy](/industries/farmers/multi-entity-farm-tax-strategy): how assets are titled and which entity holds them can determine whether a spouse's care costs put the whole operation at risk or just draw down a specific account.

## The VA Aid and Attendance benefit most veteran families never apply for

If a veteran or their surviving spouse needs help with daily activities, the [VA Aid and Attendance benefit](https://www.va.gov/pension/aid-attendance-housebound/) adds a monthly payment on top of a standard VA pension, and it can be used toward in-home care, assisted living, or a nursing facility. Brookings County has a meaningful veteran population from decades of farm families with service history, and this benefit gets missed constantly, partly because the application requires documenting both wartime service dates and unreimbursed medical expenses correctly. Getting the paperwork right the first time matters, because a rejected application can add months to the wait while care costs keep accumulating.

## Building the funding plan into your existing tax and succession strategy

The strongest long-term care plans don't exist in isolation. They get built alongside the tax and succession planning a family or business owner is already doing. Julie Underwood, CPA, works with agribusiness and professional service owners on exit and succession structures where long-term care funding is part of the same conversation: how ownership transfers, how a buyout is taxed, and how much liquidity a retiring spouse needs outside the business. Brandi Altstaetter works with multi-generational farm families on transition planning, where the question of who pays for Mom and Dad's care can otherwise turn into a fight between siblings who farm and siblings who don't.

A few of the medical costs tied to long-term care are deductible if they exceed 7.5% of adjusted gross income, including a portion of premiums for tax-qualified long-term care insurance based on age, as outlined in [IRS Publication 502](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502). That deduction alone won't fund a care plan, but it's worth building into year-round tax planning rather than discovering it in April.

This kind of planning also connects to broader financial-risk decisions families are already making, like whether they're carrying the right kind of and amount of coverage elsewhere. If you haven't looked at your overall insurance picture recently, our post on [how much insurance coverage you actually need](/resources/insuring-where-it-counts-avoid-over-insuring-in-the-wrong-plac) is a useful companion piece. And if unexpected medical costs in general are a worry, [our piece on tax-advantaged planning against medical debt](/resources/why-tax-advantaged-planning-is-the-real-defense-against-medi) walks through HSA strategy that overlaps here too.

## Common Questions

**At what age should someone buy long-term care insurance?**
Most people get the best combination of price and approval odds between ages 55 and 65, while health is still strong. Waiting until a health event forces the issue often means higher premiums, exclusions, or an outright denial, so this is a decision that rewards planning years ahead rather than reacting to a diagnosis.

**Can a farm or business be protected from long-term care costs?**
Often, yes, depending on how ownership is structured and how far in advance the planning starts. Entity structure, asset titling, and timing all matter, and Medicaid look-back rules mean transfers made too close to the need for care won't count. This is exactly the kind of planning we do alongside [multi entity farm tax strategy](/industries/farmers/multi-entity-farm-tax-strategy) work.

**How much does the VA Aid and Attendance benefit actually pay?**
The amount depends on the veteran's or surviving spouse's specific circumstances, including marital status and unreimbursed medical expenses, and it's paid in addition to the base VA pension. Full eligibility rules and current payment details are on the [VA's Aid and Attendance page](https://www.va.gov/pension/aid-attendance-housebound/).

**Is self-funding realistic without long-term care insurance?**
It can be, if the reserve is sized correctly and separated from farm or business capital that's needed to keep the operation running. A family that hasn't run those numbers is usually guessing at a figure that's too low, which is why this works best as part of a broader financial plan rather than a standalone decision.

If long-term care costs are part of a bigger conversation about your farm's succession, your business exit, or your family's overall tax strategy, [contact us](/contact) and we'll walk through what a realistic funding plan looks like for your situation.

### Unless it's working for you, your dog isn't a tax deduction
URL: /resources/unless-its-working-for-you-your-dog-isnt-a-tax-deduction-2

A client called our Brookings office last spring, half-laughing, half-serious: "My Border Collie logs more hours on this farm than I do. Can I write her off?" It's a fair question, and one we hear from farmers, kennel owners, and small business owners more often than you'd think. The honest answer is almost always no, unless the dog is genuinely working in a business. There are a handful of narrow, IRS-recognized situations where dog-related costs are legitimate deductions, and knowing the difference can save you from an audit letter down the road.

## Most dogs are a personal expense, not a deduction

The IRS treats pet expenses the same way it treats groceries or a haircut: personal, nondeductible, no exceptions for how much you love the animal. Food, grooming, vet visits, boarding, even the vet bill after your Lab decides to eat a sock, none of it counts as a business or medical expense just because the dog lives at your house or rides along in your truck.

[IRS Publication 535](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p535) sets the standard for any business expense: it has to be ordinary and necessary for carrying on your trade or business. A family pet doesn't meet that bar. Neither does the office dog who mostly naps under a desk and greets clients. Warmth and morale are real benefits, but the IRS doesn't accept "good for team spirit" as a deduction category. The dog has to be doing actual, documented work that the business depends on.

## When a farm or business dog earns a real write-off

This is where it gets interesting for our ag clients. A livestock guardian dog patrolling a pasture of 60 head of cattle outside Brookings isn't a pet in the eyes of the IRS, it's working equipment, provided the farm operates as a genuine for-profit business and files Schedule F. The same logic applies to a guard dog protecting inventory at a shop, a warehouse, or an ag supply yard, and to dogs used in a legitimate breeding operation run with the intent to profit, not a hobby litter sold to neighbors once a year.

In each of these cases, the deductible costs are the ordinary and necessary ones tied to the dog's job: food, veterinary care, training, and boarding while the animal is working. If the dog splits time between guarding the henhouse and sleeping on your kids' beds, you can only deduct the business-use portion, and you need records that back up that split. This is exactly the kind of detail our CPAs, including Julie Underwood, CPA, walk through with multi-entity farm and agribusiness clients, since a working dog on one entity's books needs to be tied clearly to that entity's income and purpose, not blended across the whole operation. If your farm runs more than one entity, our [multi-entity farm tax strategy](/industries/farmers/multi-entity-farm-tax-strategy) work covers exactly this kind of allocation question.

## Service animals get a different deduction entirely

A service animal isn't a business expense at all, it's a medical expense, and it lives on a completely different part of your return. [IRS Publication 502](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502) allows you to deduct the cost of buying, training, and maintaining a guide dog or other service animal that assists a person with a physical or mental disability. That includes food, grooming, and veterinary care, claimed as an itemized medical expense on Schedule A.

There's a catch that trips people up: medical expenses only count once your total itemized medical costs exceed 7.5% of your adjusted gross income, and only the amount above that floor is deductible. A service animal has to be trained to perform specific tasks tied to a diagnosed disability, guiding a person who is blind, alerting someone to a medical episode, retrieving items for a person with limited mobility. An emotional support animal, however comforting, generally does not meet this standard on its own.

## Therapy dogs blur the line, but the test stays the same

Therapy dog deduction questions come up a lot, and the answer depends entirely on how the dog is used. If you run a for-profit therapy practice, a physical rehab business, or a similar service where the dog is integral to the service you deliver to paying clients, the dog's costs can qualify as an ordinary business expense under the same Publication 535 standard that covers guard dogs. The dog has to be doing real, income-generating work in the business, not just sitting in the waiting room.

A personal companion dog that happens to calm you down after a hard day doesn't qualify, no matter how therapeutic the relationship feels. The IRS applies the same business-purpose test here that it applies to a guard dog on a farm: is the animal actually performing work the business depends on, and can you prove it?

## What the IRS wants to see before you claim it

Before you claim any dog-related deduction, get in the habit of separating personal costs from business costs the same way you would for a vehicle used for both hauling grain and running errands. Keep vet bills, food receipts, and training invoices specific to the working animal. A short written note on the dog's role, the hours it works, and which entity it supports goes a long way if the IRS ever asks.

| Scenario | Deduction type | Where it's claimed | What's required |
|---|---|---|---|
| Guard dog protecting shop or inventory | Business expense | Schedule C or Schedule F | Documented business purpose, for-profit operation |
| Livestock guardian dog on a working farm | Business expense | Schedule F | Farm run for profit, dog tied to herd protection |
| Legitimate breeding operation | Business expense | Schedule C | Profit motive, records, business plan |
| Service dog for a diagnosed disability | Medical expense | Schedule A, itemized | Pub 502 standard, exceeds 7.5% AGI floor |
| Therapy dog used in a for-profit practice | Business expense | Schedule C | Dog integral to services sold to clients |
| Family pet or emotional support companion | Not deductible | N/A | Personal expense, no business or medical nexus |

If your farm or service business already runs on a fixed monthly bookkeeping and tax plan through our [outsourced accounting](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting) service, this is precisely the kind of expense we flag during monthly review, not in April when it's too late to fix the paper trail. For farmers weighing which deductions are worth building documentation around, our [agriculture accounting](/who-we-serve/farmers) team can tell you fast whether a guard dog, breeding line, or working animal is worth the extra recordkeeping.

## Common Questions

**Can I deduct my dog's food and vet bills if she guards our farm shop?**
Only if guarding the shop is a documented, ongoing part of a for-profit farm business filed on Schedule F, and only for the portion of her time and costs tied to that job. If she also lives in the house as a family pet, you need to separate personal use from business use before claiming anything.

**Is a therapy dog tax deductible?**
It depends entirely on the setting. A therapy dog used in a for-profit therapy or rehab practice can qualify as a business expense under IRS Publication 535, but a personal companion dog that provides comfort at home does not qualify, even with a doctor's note.

**What's the difference between a service animal and an emotional support animal for tax purposes?**
A service animal is trained to perform specific tasks for a diagnosed disability and qualifies as a medical expense under IRS Publication 502. An emotional support animal offers comfort but isn't trained to perform tasks, so it generally does not meet the medical expense test.

**Do I need to prorate expenses if my dog is part pet, part working animal?**
Yes. The IRS expects you to allocate costs based on actual business use, similar to how you'd split a vehicle used for both farm work and personal errands. Keep a simple log of hours worked and tie vet bills or training costs to the specific role whenever possible.

If you're not sure whether your guard dog, farm dog, or breeding operation clears the bar for a real deduction, bring your numbers to our Brookings team before you file. [Contact us](/contact) and we'll walk through what's documented, what's deductible, and what to fix before next tax season.

### Why Tax-Advantaged Planning Is the Real Defense Against Medical Debt
URL: /resources/why-tax-advantaged-planning-is-the-real-defense-against-medi

A knee replacement, a cancer diagnosis, a kid's emergency surgery. Nobody plans for these, and yet almost every family we work with in Brookings faces some version of it eventually. The instinct is to build a savings cushion and hope it's enough. That's a reasonable start, but it's not a plan. The families and business owners who come through a medical crisis with their finances intact are almost always the ones who set up their tax strategy before the bill arrived, not after.

The Federal Reserve's [Report on the Economic Well-Being of U.S. Households](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/report-economic-well-being-us-households.htm) has tracked for years how many households can't absorb a $400 surprise expense without borrowing or selling something. Medical bills routinely run into the thousands, and a savings account alone rarely closes that gap. What closes it is a combination: money set aside in the right account, and a tax return built to capture every dollar the IRS already allows you to deduct.

## An emergency fund buys time, tax strategy buys relief

Cash reserves matter. Three to six months of expenses sitting in a bank account keeps a medical event from becoming a cash-flow crisis overnight. But an emergency fund is passive money. It sits there earning almost nothing and gets taxed the same whether you use it for a car repair or a hospital stay.

A Health Savings Account works differently. Contributions go in pre-tax, the balance grows tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses come out tax-free too. That's a triple tax benefit no regular savings account offers. For 2024, the IRS allows HSA contributions up to $4,150 for self-only coverage and $8,300 for family coverage, with an extra $1,000 catch-up if you're 55 or older. A farm family carrying a high-deductible health plan, which many ag operations do to control premium costs, can build a meaningful tax-advantaged reserve specifically earmarked for medical costs, separate from the general savings they're using for equipment or land payments.

Unused HSA funds roll over year after year. There's no use-it-or-lose-it deadline like with a Flexible Spending Account, which makes the HSA the better long-term tool if your health plan qualifies. An FSA still has a role for predictable annual expenses like orthodontia or contacts, but it caps out lower and typically expires the funds each year, so it's worth pairing rather than choosing one over the other.

## What counts toward your medical expense deduction

Even without an HSA, the tax code gives you a second lever: the itemized medical expense deduction. Under current law, you can deduct unreimbursed medical expenses that exceed 7.5% of your adjusted gross income, but only if you itemize instead of taking the standard deduction. [IRS Publication 502](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502) lays out exactly what qualifies, and the list is broader than most people expect: mileage to appointments, certain home modifications for a disability, long-term care premiums, even some travel costs for treatment.

Here's where the planning matters more than the deduction itself. If your medical expenses for a given year are going to land near that 7.5% threshold anyway, timing elective procedures, dental work, or vision correction into the same calendar year can push you over the line and unlock a deduction that would otherwise disappear. Spread those same expenses across two years and you might clear the threshold in neither one. This is a conversation worth having with your accountant in October, not April, because by the time you're filing, the timing decision is already gone.

## Building the plan before the bill shows up

The strongest position we see is a household or business owner running both strategies together. Money flows into an HSA throughout the year, funded automatically like a retirement contribution. A general emergency reserve sits alongside it for expenses the HSA doesn't cover, like a deductible on a disability policy or a gap in coverage during a job transition. Then, once a year, we look at whether bunching elective medical expenses into a single tax year makes sense given where the household's income landed.

For a farm operation, this gets more layered. A bad weather year can already push income down, which changes how the 7.5% AGI threshold behaves and can make medical deductions land differently than in a strong crop year. Multi-entity structures add another wrinkle, since medical expenses paid personally don't automatically flow the same way depending on how the business and the individual are set up. This is the kind of detail that gets missed when tax prep happens once a year in a rush, and it's exactly what year-round [tax planning and preparation](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting/business-tax) is built to catch.

Professional service business owners face a related version of the same problem. A single-owner practice with no HSA in place and thin cash reserves is one surgery away from a serious cash-flow disruption, on top of losing billable hours during recovery. Setting up the account structure now, before anyone needs it, is the cheap insurance most owners skip because it doesn't feel urgent until it is.

Long-term medical costs deserve their own conversation too. A short-term crisis and a long-term care need call for different tools, and we've laid out how long-term care insurance, VA Aid and Attendance benefits, and self-funding compare in our piece on [planning for long-term care costs](/resources/long-term-care-how-you-can-financially-prepare-for-the-expen). If a family member's health situation looks like it's heading toward ongoing care rather than a one-time event, that's worth reading before deciding how much to keep liquid versus how much to put toward insurance.

The common thread across every scenario: waiting until the bill arrives to think about taxes means you've already lost the ability to plan around it. We've written before about why [waiting until December to plan costs high-net-worth individuals real money](/resources/the-biggest-tax-mistake-wealthy-individuals-make-waiting-unt), and the same logic applies here at every income level. A deduction you didn't structure for doesn't show up on its own.

## Common Questions

**How much should I keep in an emergency fund versus an HSA?**
A reasonable split is three to six months of living expenses in a liquid emergency fund, with your HSA funded up to the annual limit if your health plan qualifies. The HSA money should be treated as untouchable except for medical costs, since it's the only account offering tax-free growth and tax-free withdrawals for that purpose.

**Do I need to itemize to get any tax benefit from medical expenses?**
Yes, for the medical expense deduction specifically, since it only applies if your itemized deductions exceed the standard deduction. HSA contributions are different and reduce your taxable income regardless of whether you itemize, which is one reason the HSA is usually the more reliable tax benefit for most households.

**Can I use HSA funds for a family member's medical bills?**
You can use HSA funds for your spouse and any tax dependents, even if they're not covered under your specific high-deductible health plan. Keep receipts, since the IRS can ask for documentation showing the withdrawal went toward a qualified expense listed in Publication 502.

**What happens if my medical expenses don't hit the 7.5% AGI threshold?**
If they don't, you get no deduction for that year under current law, which is exactly why timing elective procedures matters. Bunching predictable expenses like dental work or new glasses into a year when you're already near the threshold, rather than spreading them out, is a decision your accountant can help you time before December 31.

If a medical event, an aging parent's care needs, or just the uncertainty of not having a plan has been sitting in the back of your mind, [reach out to our team](/contact) and we'll walk through what an HSA, your deduction picture, and your reserve fund should actually look like for your situation.

### Auto Leasing vs. Buying: Which Makes More Sense?
URL: /resources/auto-leasing-vs-buying-which-makes-more-sense-2

Every dealership in Brookings will steer you toward the payment that feels smaller today. Every online calculator will tell you buying builds equity, full stop. Neither one knows your tax bracket, your annual mileage, or whether that vehicle sits on your Schedule C, your S-corp's books, or your personal checking account. That's the piece missing from most lease vs buy a car comparisons, and it's usually where the real money is.

## The question underneath the payment

For an individual buying a personal vehicle with zero business use, this decision mostly comes down to cash flow and how long you keep cars. Trade every three years and hate surprise repair bills? Leasing has real appeal. Drive a vehicle into the ground at 150,000 miles? Buying wins almost every time.

For a farm running a truck 40,000 miles a year hauling grain and livestock, or a professional service business titling a vehicle to the company, the calculation changes. Business vehicle purchase vs lease decisions carry tax consequences that can shift the total cost by thousands of dollars in the first year alone, before you even factor in what happens at trade-in.

## How the payment stacks up over five years

Here's a simplified look at a $45,000 crew cab truck, financed at 7% over 60 months versus leased on a comparable 36-month term.

| | Leasing | Buying with a loan |
|---|---|---|
| Typical monthly payment | Lower, often $550-650 | Higher, often $850-900 |
| Ownership at the end | None, unless you exercise a buyout | Full ownership |
| Mileage limits | 10,000-15,000 miles/year, overage fees apply | None |
| Maintenance | Often covered under factory warranty | Owner's responsibility once warranty ends |
| Business tax treatment | Deduct the business-use percentage of lease payments as paid | Depreciate the cost, possibly with Section 179 |

Over five years, that lease might run roughly $37,000 in total payments with nothing to show for it afterward. The loan runs closer to $53,000, but you're left holding a truck worth $15,000 to $20,000 at trade-in. Run the numbers on your specific vehicle and mileage before assuming either side wins by default.

## Section 179 tips the scale for business vehicles

If a vehicle is used more than 50% for business, buying opens a door leasing doesn't: accelerated depreciation. Under the rules outlined in [IRS Publication 946](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p946), heavy vehicles, generally those over 6,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, qualify for a substantially larger first-year Section 179 vehicle deduction than passenger cars, which are capped under separate luxury-auto depreciation limits.

Say a farmer buys a $55,000 crew cab used 80% for hauling feed and equipment. Depending on the year's limits and the owner's tax bracket, that Section 179 election could reduce the current-year tax bill by $8,000 to $12,000. Lease that same truck and you only deduct the business-use portion of the payments as they're made, spread thin over the lease term instead of taken up front. The tradeoff: buying locks you into ownership and depreciation recapture rules if you sell early, so this is a decision worth modeling with your CPA before you sign anything, not after.

Entity structure matters here too. A vehicle titled to a farm LLC versus held personally changes how the deduction flows through, which is part of why [entity type analysis](/what-we-do/advisory-services/entity-type-analysis) tends to come up in the same conversation as vehicle purchases.

## Mileage habits decide more than the tax code does

A farmer or ag operator logging 30,000 to 50,000 miles a year on rural roads and gravel, hauling trailers and equipment, will blow past lease mileage caps almost every year. Overage charges commonly run $0.15 to $0.25 per mile, which turns a good-looking lease payment into an expensive mistake by year two.

Compare that to a professional service business owner driving under 10,000 miles a year for client meetings around Brookings. Lower mileage, lighter wear, and a preference for a newer vehicle every few years can make leasing the more sensible pick, especially when the vehicle isn't central to how the business earns revenue.

## What this looks like for farmers, agribusiness, and service businesses

Farm and agribusiness operations usually lean toward buying. Heavy trucks, high annual mileage, and Section 179 eligibility stack in favor of ownership, and the equipment often outlasts the loan term by years. This is a regular part of the [tax preparation and planning](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting/business-tax) conversations we have with row crop and livestock operations across South Dakota.

Professional service businesses, from consulting firms to real estate offices, tend to have more flexibility. Lower mileage and less wear-and-tear make leasing viable, particularly for owners who value predictable payments over long-term ownership. If the vehicle is a minor part of overall business assets, the simplicity of leasing can outweigh the tax advantage of buying. It's worth reviewing this alongside your broader [accounting services for service-based businesses](/who-we-serve/professional-service-businesses) rather than deciding on the vehicle in isolation.

## Run the cash flow test before you sign

Interest rates on auto loans move with the broader credit market, and the [Federal Reserve's Consumer Credit (G.19) report](https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/current/) tracks how those rates shift over time. A loan that penciled out favorably eighteen months ago may not today, which is a good reason to run the actual after-tax cost of both options before committing to financing over leasing, or the reverse.

The monthly payment is the easiest number to compare and the least useful one on its own. What matters is the after-tax cost per mile driven, factoring in depreciation, interest, maintenance, and how the vehicle is titled. That's a five-minute conversation with a CPA who already knows your entity structure and tax situation, not a spreadsheet you build alone the night before you sign.

## Common Questions

**Is leasing or buying better for a small business vehicle?**
It depends on mileage and business-use percentage. High-mileage, heavy-use vehicles like farm trucks usually favor buying because of Section 179 eligibility and no mileage caps. Lower-mileage vehicles for client meetings or light delivery often lease more affordably, especially if you replace vehicles every few years.

**Can I deduct lease payments on my taxes?**
Yes, but only the business-use percentage. If you use a leased vehicle 70% for business, you deduct 70% of the lease payment along with 70% of related operating costs like fuel and insurance, based on mileage logs that support that percentage.

**What's the Section 179 vehicle deduction limit?**
Limits vary by year and vehicle weight class, with heavier vehicles (over 6,000 pounds gross vehicle weight) eligible for a much larger first-year deduction than passenger cars. Details are outlined in [IRS Publication 946](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p946), and current-year limits should be confirmed before you purchase.

**Does a farm truck qualify for Section 179?**
Most farm trucks used over 50% for business qualify, provided the business-use percentage is documented. Weight class affects how much you can deduct in year one, which is why crew cab and heavy-duty trucks common on South Dakota operations often see the largest first-year benefit.

If you're weighing a vehicle purchase or lease for your farm, agribusiness, or service business, [contact TruCount CPA PC](/contact) before you sign. We'll run the after-tax numbers on both options against your actual entity structure and mileage, so the decision holds up past the first year.

### Take Back Control of Subscription Creep
URL: /resources/take-back-control-of-subscription-creep-2

A grain marketing platform at $79 a month. A yield-mapping subscription your agronomist recommended two seasons ago and nobody's opened since. Three project management tools your office manager tried before settling on one, except the other two never got canceled. A payroll add-on nobody uses anymore, and a QuickBooks tier purchased during a growth spurt that's now more software than the business needs. None of these charges looks dramatic sitting alone on a statement. Stacked together, on a farm operation or a service business with a healthy checking account, they can quietly run $400 to $1,200 a month, whether or not a single person opens the app that month. That's subscription creep, and it deserves the same scrutiny as fuel, feed, or payroll, not a shrug at tax time.

## Subscription creep is a cash flow problem, not a nuisance

Most owners treat recurring software charges as background noise, something too small to argue about compared to a combine payment or a lease renewal. That's exactly why it grows. A $30 tool approved in 2022 becomes a $65 tool in 2025 after two price increases nobody noticed, because the charge auto-renews on a card that's rarely reconciled line by line. Multiply that across ten or fifteen tools and the number stops being trivial. The Federal Reserve's [Consumer & Community Context](https://www.federalreserve.gov/consumerscommunities.htm) research tracks exactly this pattern at the household level: small, recurring costs compound in ways people consistently underestimate until they're forced to look closely. The same math applies to a business checking account. A dollar spent on an unused tool every month for a year is a real dollar, and it's one that didn't go toward debt paydown, equipment reserves, or a bonus for the employee who's been carrying extra weight.

## Why farm and service business books hide it so well

Subscription creep is worse in agriculture and professional services than in most industries, and there's a structural reason for it. Farm operations often run multiple entities, a crop LLC, a cattle operation, maybe a trucking arm, each with its own bank account and its own set of software tools nobody's cross-checked in years. Precision ag platforms, drone imagery services, and soil-sampling subscriptions get added field by field, season by season, and rarely get pruned back once the trial is over. Professional service firms have the mirror problem: every new hire gets their own login to two or three SaaS tools, and when that employee leaves, the subscription often doesn't. If your farm uses precision-ag or yield-data subscriptions to test a new fertility program or seed variety, keep every invoice. That documentation can support [R&D tax credit](/what-we-do/advisory-services/r-and-d-tax-credits) claims for qualifying on-farm trials, which means a subscription you're already paying for might do double duty instead of just draining cash.

## Run a subscription audit like a cost-of-production report

Farmers already know how to break down cost per acre or cost per head. A subscription audit works the same way: pull every recurring charge, assign it to the entity and the person responsible, and decide whether it's earning its keep.

| Step | What to do |
|---|---|
| Pull 90 days of statements | Bank accounts and every business card, not just the one you check most |
| List every recurring charge | Vendor, amount, billing cycle, and which entity or department owns it |
| Assign an owner | Someone accountable for saying whether it's still used |
| Check usage, not intent | Log-in frequency or feature use, not whether it sounded useful at signup |
| Decide: keep, renegotiate, or cancel | Annual plans often get 15-20% off if you just ask before renewal |
| Calendar the next review | 90 days out, tied to your renewal dates, not a vague "someday" |

A farm with three entities and a service business with twelve employees will each find a different number of leaks, but almost everyone finds something. The habit matters more than the audit itself. A [money mindset](/resources/your-money-mindset-is-costing-your-small-business-more-than) that treats recurring charges as fixed, unquestionable overhead is usually the real reason the audit didn't happen sooner.

## Where a monthly review catches what an annual one misses

An annual cleanup helps, but it means twelve months of leakage before anyone looks. Reconciliation done monthly, as part of ongoing bookkeeping, flags a new recurring charge the month it appears, not the month you finally decide to dig through a year of statements. That's part of why our [accounting services](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting/accounting) include line-by-line reconciliation on every account tied to your business, not just the one your bookkeeper happens to check.

Expense analysis is also a standing piece of our [advisory services](/what-we-do/advisory-services), bundled into the same fixed monthly fee as bookkeeping and tax planning, so there's no separate invoice every time we flag a subscription that's outlived its usefulness. You see the same numbers we do, in real time, through the same online platform, rather than waiting for a year-end summary to explain where the cash went. The AICPA's [personal financial planning resources](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/resources/landing/personal-financial-planning) make a similar case for individuals: recurring costs deserve the same ongoing review as any other line in a household budget, not a once-a-year glance.

## Common questions

**How do I know if my business has subscription creep?**
If you can't list every recurring charge on your business accounts from memory, you likely have some. A quick test: pull last month's statements and count how many charges you couldn't explain in one sentence. Most owners find at least two or three tools they forgot they were paying for.

**How often should I audit recurring expenses?**
Quarterly works well for most farms and service businesses, timed around your reconciliation cycle. Seasonal operations should also check right before planting or harvest, when ag-specific software renewals tend to cluster and get approved without a second look.

**Can bookkeeping software catch subscription creep automatically?**
Software can flag recurring transactions, but it can't tell you whether the tool is still worth paying for. That judgment call needs a person looking at usage against cost, which is why reconciliation paired with an actual review, not just categorization, is what catches the waste.

**Are business subscriptions tax deductible?**
Most software and service subscriptions used for business purposes are deductible as ordinary business expenses. The complication is mixed-use tools split across personal and business accounts, or subscriptions tied to a specific entity in a multi-entity farm structure, where the deduction needs to land on the right return.

If your bank statements have more recurring charges than you can name off the top of your head, that's worth twenty minutes on a call before your next renewal cycle hits. [Contact TruCount CPA PC](/contact) and we'll walk through what a real subscription audit looks like for your farm or business, bundled into the same fixed monthly relationship we already use to keep your books current.

### Labor Cost Management for Small Business in a Rebalancing Market
URL: /resources/the-great-rebalancing-why-the-new-labor-market-demands-a-fin-2

For two years, owners in Brookings and across the Midwest hired anyone who showed up, paid whatever it took to keep a crew intact through harvest, and treated a 15 percent raise as the cost of staying open. That era is easing. Quit rates are back near pre-2021 levels, applicant pools are deeper, and the frantic bidding wars for entry-level help have mostly stopped. But here's the part owners miss: the wages you raised in 2022 didn't come back down, and your payroll budget is still built on panic-era assumptions instead of a real plan. Labor cost management isn't an HR project anymore. It's a financial planning problem, and it belongs on the same table as your tax projections and your cash flow forecast.

This matters whether you're running 900 acres near Volga, managing a three-location ag retail operation, or billing hours out of a professional services office on Main Avenue. Labor is usually the largest controllable expense on the income statement, and it's the one most owners still manage by feel.

## Why a calmer labor market still costs you money

A cooling labor market doesn't mean cheaper labor. It means the emergency raises you handed out to stop the bleeding are now permanent, embedded in your base pay scale, and compounding every time you run an annual increase on top of them. A shop that bumped a $16 starting wage to $19 in 2022 to compete for hires isn't rolling that back now that applications are up. The new floor is $19, plus whatever cost-of-living bump gets layered on next year.

Meanwhile, benefits costs, workers' comp premiums, and payroll tax obligations scale with that higher wage base. So the real story of 2024 and 2025 isn't wage growth easing. It's wage growth easing while the elevated base from the last few years locks in as your new normal. If your budgeting still treats labor as "whatever it costs to fill the position," you're planning around a number that's already out of date the moment you write it down.

## What retention actually costs when you run the math

Most owners can tell you their turnover rate but not what it costs them. Run the numbers on a single departure: recruiting time, onboarding, lost productivity while a new hire ramps up, and overtime paid to cover the gap. For a skilled ag mechanic or an experienced bookkeeper, replacement cost commonly runs 20 to 30 percent of that role's annual pay once you count the ramp-up period, not just the ad spend and interview hours.

That reframes retention as a financial decision, not a culture initiative. A $2,000 retention bonus paid to a key seasonal crew lead who's stayed three years in a row is cheap compared to a spring scramble to find, train, and trust a stranger during planting. Professional service firms see the same math with client-facing staff: the cost of losing someone who knows your clients' history isn't just payroll, it's billable hours that don't get billed while someone new gets up to speed.

## Building labor cost into your books instead of your gut

Most small businesses track labor as one line: payroll expense. That tells you what you spent, not whether it's sustainable. A better approach breaks labor into a few numbers you actually watch monthly:

| Metric | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Labor cost as % of revenue | Whether pay is scaling with the business or outrunning it |
| Labor cost per unit (per acre, per head, per billable hour) | Whether efficiency is improving or slipping |
| Overtime as % of total payroll | Whether you're understaffed or mismanaging scheduling |
| Cost per hire vs. retention bonus cost | Whether it's cheaper to keep people or replace them |

For a grain operation, that might mean tracking labor cost per acre across planting, spraying, and harvest separately, since a $19-an-hour operator running a $400,000 combine during an eight-day harvest window is a very different cost decision than the same wage paid for winter maintenance work. For a professional service firm, it means comparing staff cost to realized billing rate by role, not just total payroll against total revenue.

This kind of reporting is exactly what we build into a client's monthly numbers through our [advisory services](/what-we-do/advisory-services), which includes payroll analysis and revenue analysis as standard, not an add-on. When labor cost has its own line and its own trend, a wage decision stops being a gut call made in the break room and becomes a number you can actually plan a season around.

## Ag employers face a different version of the same problem

Seasonal and ag labor budgeting has its own wrinkles: overtime rules that don't apply the same way to agricultural workers, H-2A wage rate requirements that shift annually, and payroll that spikes hard for six weeks and disappears for six months. A crew of eight during harvest and two during January isn't a staffing plan, it's a cash flow event, and it needs to be modeled as one well before the first check gets cut.

We handle payroll processing for farm and agribusiness clients with exactly this rhythm in mind, including multi-state crews and seasonal wage changes, through our [payroll services](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting/payroll). If your operation runs multiple entities, a family farm alongside a custom application business, for example, labor cost planning also intersects with how those entities are structured for tax purposes. That's worth a look through our [multi-entity farm tax strategy](/industries/farmers/multi-entity-farm-tax-strategy) guidance if you haven't reviewed your structure in the last few years.

Professional service owners have a parallel version of this: the temptation to hire ahead of revenue because good people are finally available again. That instinct isn't wrong, but it needs a budget behind it, not just an open req. If staffing decisions keep getting made on adrenaline instead of a plan, that's usually a sign the underlying money habits need attention before the hiring plan will hold, something we get into in [Your Money Mindset Is Costing Your Small Business More Than Your Budget Ever Will](/resources/your-money-mindset-is-costing-your-small-business-more-than).

## Turning this into a workforce budgeting strategy

A workforce budget worth having answers three questions before you post a job or hand out a raise: What does this role cost fully loaded, not just in base pay? What's the retention cost if this person leaves in year one versus year three? And what does labor need to look like as a percentage of revenue for the business to hit its margin target this year? The SBA's [guide to hiring and managing employees](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/manage-your-business/hire-manage-employees) is a solid starting point for the compliance side of this, covering classification, recordkeeping, and the basics of what the law requires as you add staff.

The financial side is where most owners get stuck, because it requires real-time numbers, not a spreadsheet updated once a year at tax time. That's the gap a bundled, fixed-fee accounting relationship is built to close. Instead of finding out in March that labor ran 34 percent of revenue instead of the 28 percent you budgeted, you see it drift in June, while there's still time to adjust hiring, pricing, or scheduling before it eats the year's profit.

## Common Questions

**Is wage growth actually slowing down for small businesses in 2024 and 2025?**
Hiring pressure has eased compared to 2021 and 2022, with more applicants per opening and fewer bidding wars for entry-level roles. But the wage increases made during the tight labor market mostly aren't reversing, so total labor cost stays elevated even as the pace of new increases slows.

**How do I know if my labor costs are too high?**
Compare labor cost as a percentage of revenue against your own trend over the last three years, not an industry average pulled from a blog. If that percentage is climbing while revenue growth is flat, the problem usually isn't wages, it's scheduling, overtime, or a staffing level built for a busier season than the one you're in.

**Does it make financial sense to pay a retention bonus instead of hiring someone new?**
Often yes, especially for roles where training time is long or client relationships matter. A retention bonus equal to 5 to 10 percent of annual pay is frequently cheaper than the 20 to 30 percent replacement cost tied to recruiting, onboarding, and lost productivity during a transition.

**Should ag employers budget labor differently than professional service businesses?**
Yes. Ag labor is seasonal and tied to weather-driven windows like planting and harvest, so cash flow planning needs to account for short, intense payroll spikes. Professional service firms usually carry more level staffing but need to track labor cost against billable hours and realized rate instead of raw revenue.

If your payroll budget still reflects panic-era hiring instead of where the labor market actually sits today, [contact us](/contact) and we'll walk through what a real workforce budget looks like for your operation, ag or professional service, before your next hiring or wage decision gets made on a guess.

### Your Money Mindset Is Costing Your Small Business More Than Your Budget Ever Will
URL: /resources/your-money-mindset-is-costing-your-small-business-more-than

A farmer we work with in Brookings County used to avoid opening his year-end financials until his tax appointment forced the issue. He wasn't disorganized. He knew his equipment costs, his grain prices, his input spend, off the top of his head. What he avoided was the feeling of seeing it all added up. That's not a bookkeeping problem. That's a money mindset problem, and it costs more in missed deductions, underpriced work, and reactive decisions than most owners realize.

We see this pattern across farms, agribusinesses, and service companies alike: the books get fixed before the psychology does, and six months later the same cash crunch shows up again. A clean chart of accounts doesn't change how an owner feels about looking at a bank balance mid-February. If the underlying discomfort with money never gets addressed, better software just produces prettier numbers that still go unread.

## The behaviors that quietly drain a small business

Money mindset isn't a personality trait. It shows up as specific, repeatable behaviors, and most owners can recognize themselves in at least two or three of these:

- Pricing jobs or crops based on what feels fair rather than what the math says is sustainable
- Avoiding financial statements until a tax deadline or loan application forces a look
- Making equipment, hiring, or expansion decisions reactively, in response to a good season or a scare, instead of against a plan
- Treating cash in the account as available profit, regardless of what's owed in taxes or payroll
- Delaying a hard conversation about entity structure, succession, or an exit because it feels premature

Each of these has a dollar cost attached. Underpricing service work by even 8 to 10 percent compounds across every invoice for a year. Avoiding financial statements means quarterly tax estimates get built on guesswork instead of actual year-to-date profit, which is how owners end up with a April surprise instead of a plan. The [SBA's guidance on managing your finances](https://www.sba.gov/business-guide/manage-your-business/manage-your-finances) puts it plainly: financial management isn't a once-a-year event, it's an ongoing discipline, and that discipline is where mindset and bookkeeping meet.

## Why fixing the books alone doesn't fix the plateau

We've set up clean accounting systems for farm operations that were still stuck in the same spot a year later, because the owner still made every big decision from anxiety rather than data. The books were accurate. Nobody looked at them until something went wrong. That's the plateau: revenue holds steady, margins stay thin, and growth decisions get made in a rush instead of with room to think.

A multi-entity farm operation we've worked with had three separate LLCs and a pattern of moving cash between them whenever one entity felt tight, without tracking the transfers as loans or distributions. The result wasn't fraud, it was avoidance. Looking closely at three sets of books at once felt overwhelming, so nobody did. Once we built a [multi-entity farm tax strategy](/industries/farmers/multi-entity-farm-tax-strategy) with clear intercompany accounting, the anxiety dropped because the picture became visible instead of vague. Visibility is usually what breaks the cycle, not willpower.

## Three mindset shifts that change the numbers

**Treat the monthly financial review as non-negotiable, not optional.** Owners who look at revenue, expenses, and cash flow every month, even for fifteen minutes, catch a margin slip in June instead of discovering it in December. This is the core of what we deliver in [advisory services](/what-we-do/advisory-services): budgeting, revenue analysis, and cash flow analysis delivered on a schedule, so looking at the numbers becomes routine instead of dreaded.

**Separate the emotion of a bad season from the facts of a bad decision.** A rough crop year or a slow quarter for a service business doesn't automatically mean the pricing or the entity structure is wrong. Sometimes it does. The only way to know the difference is to have real numbers in front of you, which is why an [entity type analysis](/what-we-do/advisory-services/entity-type-analysis) or a fresh look at labor costs, like the guidance in our piece on [labor cost management for small business](/resources/the-great-rebalancing-why-the-new-labor-market-demands-a-fin), should happen on a plan, not in a panic.

**Stop treating tax planning as a once-a-year event.** Owners with a scarcity mindset around money tend to make tax decisions in December or, worse, in April, because looking at tax exposure earlier feels like inviting bad news. Waiting rarely produces a better outcome. Our piece on [tax planning for high-net-worth individuals](/resources/the-biggest-tax-mistake-wealthy-individuals-make-waiting-unt) makes the same case that applies here: the cost of waiting is almost always higher than the cost of looking early.

## What a healthy money mindset actually looks like day to day

It's not confidence for its own sake. It's a set of habits:

| Habit | What it replaces |
|---|---|
| Monthly review of revenue, COGS, and cash flow | Reviewing numbers only at tax time |
| Pricing based on documented cost and margin targets | Pricing based on what competitors charge or what feels comfortable |
| Quarterly estimated tax planning tied to actual year-to-date profit | Guessing at estimates or skipping them until a penalty shows up |
| Treating owner draws as separate from operating cash | Pulling cash whenever the account looks full |
| Reviewing entity structure every few years as the business grows | Keeping the original structure indefinitely by default |

The [AICPA's small business resources](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/resources/landing/small-business-resources) reinforce a similar point: financial literacy and consistent habits, not one big fix, are what separate businesses that grow steadily from ones that stall and restart every few years.

## Where a CPA relationship actually changes the behavior, not just the books

Bundling bookkeeping, payroll, and advisory into one fixed monthly fee does more than simplify billing. It removes the friction that keeps owners from asking questions. When a client isn't worried about a surprise invoice for every phone call, they call sooner, before a small pricing mistake becomes a full quarter of underbilled work. That's the reasoning behind our [outsourced accounting](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting) model: real-time access to numbers through a secure online platform, paired with someone who actually knows the operation, so looking at the books stops feeling like an audit and starts feeling like a conversation.

Julie Underwood, CPA, works with agribusiness owners running multiple entities who've spent years avoiding a clear look at how those entities interact for tax purposes. The fix usually isn't more software. It's a structured conversation about what the numbers mean and a plan for reviewing them regularly, which is exactly what turns a good bookkeeping system into a habit an owner actually uses.

## Common Questions

**What is a money mindset, in practical business terms?**
It's the set of beliefs and habits that shape how an owner reacts to financial information, whether they check numbers regularly or avoid them, price confidently or apologetically, and plan ahead or react after the fact. Two businesses with identical books can have very different outcomes based on which habits the owner practices.

**Can better bookkeeping fix a bad money mindset on its own?**
Not by itself. Clean books make accurate information available, but if an owner still avoids looking at that information or makes decisions from anxiety instead of data, the underlying pattern continues. Pairing accurate books with a regular review habit, ideally monthly, is what changes outcomes.

**How often should a small business owner actually look at their numbers?**
Monthly, at minimum, for revenue, expenses, and cash flow, with a deeper quarterly review tied to estimated tax planning. Waiting until tax season means every decision that quarter was made on old information.

**Does this apply to farms as much as service businesses?**
Yes, arguably more, because farm income is seasonal and irregular, which makes it easier to avoid looking at numbers during the off months. Farmers who review cash position and entity structure year-round, not just at harvest or tax time, catch deduction opportunities and pricing issues earlier.

If the same cash flow worry or pricing hesitation has shown up again this year, the fix probably isn't another spreadsheet. It's a regular, judgment-free look at your actual numbers with someone who already understands farm and service business finances. [Reach out through our contact page](/contact) and let's find the habit that's been missing.
